title: Choosing Compute, Storage, and Network Building Blocks
bodyMarkdown:
## Compute: pick the most managed service that meets the requirement

The Well-Architected [system design principles](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/system-design) tell you to simplify and use managed services, and to prefer stateless designs. Applied to compute: start at the top of the table and move down only when a concrete requirement forces you to.

| Service | Choose when | Avoid when |
|---------|-------------|------------|
| **Cloud Run** (services, jobs, worker pools) | Stateless containers, HTTP APIs and microservices, run-to-completion jobs, pull-based background workers; scale to zero; pay for use | You need Kubernetes-level control of Pod placement, privileged workloads or cluster configuration |
| **Cloud Run functions** | Small event-driven code that glues services together | A long-lived, multi-component service |
| **GKE Autopilot** | Kubernetes API and ecosystem needed, Google manages nodes and scaling; Google's recommended default mode for most GKE workloads | Workloads that need privileges or configuration Autopilot does not allow |
| **GKE Standard** | Granular control over cluster settings, node pools, Pod placement, special privileges | You do not need that control (you take on node operations for nothing) |
| **Compute Engine (MIGs)** | Lift-and-shift, custom OS or kernel, licensing tied to VMs, special hardware, full control | You want zero infrastructure operations |

[Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) offers four resource types: services answer HTTP requests behind a unique HTTPS endpoint and autoscale; jobs run to completion; worker pools run continuous pull-based work such as Pub/Sub or Kafka consumers and are scaled manually; instances (preview) are for long-lived singleton runtimes. Idle services scale down to zero instances, and billing is either request-based (no idle charge) or instance-based (charged for the instance lifetime).

The GKE [mode guidance](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/choose-cluster-mode) is explicit: use Autopilot for most workloads unless your application needs privileges or configuration that Autopilot constraints do not allow. In Autopilot, GKE manages the cluster infrastructure including nodes and scaling; in Standard you configure node pools and scaling yourself.

Exam heuristic: a scenario with dozens of interdependent services, custom networking, a service mesh, GPU inference and fine-grained scheduling across hundreds of nodes is a GKE scenario; a single new stateless container that must scale to zero and avoid cluster upgrades is a Cloud Run scenario. A "single large VM running Docker Compose" is never the answer for a platform that needs orchestration.

### Compute cost levers

- **Spot VMs.** Discounts of up to 91% for many machine types, GPUs, TPUs and Local SSDs, per the [Spot VM documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot). Spot VMs have no minimum or maximum runtime unless you set one, are not guaranteed to be available, and are excluded from the Compute Engine SLA. The preemption notice defaults to 0 seconds and can be configured up to 120 seconds. They are the successor to preemptible VMs. Use for fault-tolerant batch and stateless work; make tasks idempotent and checkpointed.
- **Committed use discounts.** Per the [CUD overview](https://cloud.google.com/docs/cuds), resource-based CUDs cover Compute Engine resources in a region, while spend-based CUDs cover a minimum dollar commitment (compute flexible commitments span Compute Engine, GKE and Cloud Run). Terms are one or three years and you are billed monthly for the commitment whether or not you use it, so commit only to the steady baseline, never to peak or bursty capacity.
- **Right-sizing.** Compute Engine [machine type recommendations](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/apply-machine-type-recommendations-for-instances) are based on the previous 8 days of Cloud Monitoring metrics and can suggest a standard or custom machine type. They are not shown when savings are below $10 per month and are unavailable for memory-optimized families and instances with GPUs or TPUs.
- **Scale to zero when idle.** Cloud Run does it natively. A MIG can scale in to zero only with schedule-based autoscaling and `minNumReplicas` set to 0; per the [autoscaler documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/autoscaler), a MIG autoscaled on CPU utilization, HTTP load balancing capacity or per-instance monitoring metrics cannot reach zero.

## Storage: match the data shape and access pattern

| Need | Service | Key point |
|------|---------|-----------|
| Objects, media, backups, data lake | **Cloud Storage** | Unlimited storage, four cold-to-hot classes, lifecycle rules |
| Shared POSIX file system over NFS | **Filestore** | Mountable by many VMs and GKE concurrently |
| Block storage for a VM | **Persistent Disk** | Attached to VMs; snapshots for backup |
| Relational, regional, MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server | **Cloud SQL** | Fully managed; HA is zonal |
| Relational, global scale, strong consistency | **Spanner** | Horizontal scale with SQL and ACID transactions |
| Wide-column NoSQL, huge throughput, time series | **Bigtable** | No SQL joins or multi-row transactions |
| Document store for mobile and web apps | **Firestore** | Serverless, real-time sync, transactions |
| Analytics warehouse | **BigQuery** | Analytical queries rather than OLTP |

[Spanner](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/) combines relational SQL and ACID transactions with strong consistency and horizontal scalability, and multi-region configurations (99.999% SLA, replicas across regions) make it the fit for a globally distributed inventory that needs strongly consistent writes. [Cloud SQL](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/introduction) is a managed service for MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server: right for regional relational workloads and for lift-and-shift of those engines, but its HA does not span regions. [Bigtable](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/overview) scales to billions of rows and is suited to time-series, IoT and large-throughput workloads; Google points to Firestore for structured documents with ACID transactions and BigQuery for analytics. [Firestore](https://cloud.google.com/firestore) is a serverless document database with native mobile and web SDKs and real-time synchronization.

### Cloud Storage classes

The [storage classes](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes) differ in price structure and minimum storage duration, not in access latency: every class serves data with millisecond latency, including Archive.

| Class | Intended access | Minimum storage duration | Notes |
|-------|----------------|--------------------------|-------|
| **Standard** | Frequent | None | 99.9% regional SLA, 99.95% multi-region |
| **Nearline** | About once a month or less | 30 days | Retrieval fees; 99.0% regional SLA |
| **Coldline** | About once a quarter or less | 90 days | Higher retrieval cost than Nearline |
| **Archive** | Long-term archive, rarely read | 365 days | Lowest storage price; data still available within milliseconds |

Rapid Storage, a newer class limited to zonal buckets for I/O-intensive workloads, also exists; it is performance-oriented rather than a cold tier. For seven-year audit logs read about once a year, Archive minimizes cost, and "retrievable within hours" does not rule it out.

Use [Object Lifecycle Management](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle) to automate this. Actions are Delete, SetStorageClass (only to equal or colder classes, for example Standard to Nearline to Coldline to Archive) and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload. Conditions include age, createdBefore, numNewerVersions, prefix and suffix matches and size; all conditions in a rule must match. Actions run asynchronously, and lifecycle configuration changes can take up to 24 hours to apply.

### Filestore

[Filestore tiers](https://cloud.google.com/filestore/docs/service-tiers) are Zonal (1 TiB to 100 TiB, aimed at HPC and localized workloads), Regional (100 GiB to 100 TiB, for regional resilience) and Enterprise with multishares for GKE (1 TiB to 10 TiB). They support NFSv3 and NFSv4.1 with backups, snapshots and replication. Basic HDD and Basic SSD remain as legacy tiers. A rendering farm of VMs and a GKE cluster that must share a POSIX file system is a Filestore question, not a Cloud Storage FUSE or single Persistent Disk question.

## Network: connectivity, privacy and load balancing

**VPC fundamentals.** Per the [VPC documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc), a VPC network and its routes and firewall rules are global, while subnets are regional. New projects get a default auto mode network with one subnet per region from 10.128.0.0/9. Custom mode, where you create subnets and ranges yourself, is the recommended choice for production, and the conversion from auto to custom is one-way. Each primary subnet range reserves four unusable IP addresses. Plan CIDRs across VPCs and on-premises before connecting anything.

**Private connectivity options.**

| Option | What it does | IP overlap | Transitive |
|--------|-------------|------------|-----------|
| **[VPC Network Peering](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering)** | Exchanges routes between two VPCs | Not allowed: no subnet range may match, contain or fit within a peer's range | No |
| **[Private Service Connect](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/private-service-connect)** | Consumer reaches a producer service through an internal IP endpoint in its own VPC | Allowed: NAT removes any IP coordination between consumer and producer | Not applicable |
| **[Cloud NAT](https://cloud.google.com/nat/docs/overview)** | Outbound translation so VMs, GKE, Cloud Run and App Engine standard need no external IPs | n/a | n/a |

Private Service Connect supports endpoints and backends for Google APIs such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery, and published services from Google, third parties or other teams in your organization via service attachments. Cloud NAT is regional, configured per region and subnet, and does not allow unsolicited inbound connections, so it cannot expose a service.

**Hybrid connectivity.** The [connectivity product guide](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/how-to/choose-product) lists HA VPN (IPsec over the internet; 99.99% or 99.9% SLA depending on topology), Dedicated Interconnect (10, 100 or 400 Gbps circuits, VLAN attachments from 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps, up to 8 circuits per connection), Partner Interconnect (50 Mbps to 50 Gbps per attachment through a provider) and Cross-Cloud Interconnect for other clouds.

**Load balancing.** From the [load balancer overview](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/load-balancing-overview): global external Application Load Balancers use a single anycast IP with multi-region backends; regional external ones are single-region and available in both Network Service Tiers; internal Application Load Balancers are reachable only inside the VPC (regional or cross-region). Network Load Balancers work at layer 4, either proxy-based or passthrough; passthrough preserves client source IPs with direct server return. Premium Tier uses Google's global backbone and supports global load balancers; Standard Tier routes over the public internet and is regional, trading performance for cost.

## Decision approach

1. Extract the NFRs: latency, scale, consistency, availability, residency.
2. Choose storage from data shape and access pattern; the database choice is the hardest to change later.
3. Choose the most managed compute that satisfies the control requirements.
4. Layer networking: load balancer for HA, PSC for private service access, NAT for egress, Interconnect or VPN for hybrid.
5. Apply cost levers last: Spot for fault-tolerant work, CUDs for steady baselines, lifecycle rules for storage.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **GKE by default.** Running a single simple stateless service on a cluster adds node and upgrade operations for no benefit.
- **Cloud Run for everything,** including workloads that need privileged containers or Kubernetes primitives.
- **Spot for stateful or deadline-bound work** with no checkpointing; Spot VMs carry no SLA.
- **CUDs sized to peak.** You pay for the commitment whether or not you use it.
- **Cloud Storage as a shared POSIX file system.** Use Filestore when applications need file semantics.
- **Bigtable for relational needs** or Cloud SQL for global write scale.
- **Choosing Nearline or Coldline for data that is read often,** where retrieval fees and minimum durations erase the savings, or Archive for objects deleted within a year.
- **Peering with overlapping ranges,** or expecting peering to be transitive.
- **Cloud NAT as an ingress path.**
- **Auto mode networks in production,** and overlapping on-premises ranges discovered after the Interconnect is ordered.

## Exam tips

- **Most managed that fits.** New stateless container, scale to zero, no node management: Cloud Run. Many interdependent services needing mesh, custom networking and GPU scheduling: GKE.
- **Autopilot is the default GKE recommendation;** pick Standard only for privileges or configuration Autopilot does not allow.
- **Shared POSIX across VMs and GKE is Filestore;** Persistent Disk is block storage for a VM and Cloud Storage is object storage.
- **Global, strongly consistent, relational with horizontal write scale is Spanner.** Bigtable is for key-based wide-column throughput without joins; Cloud SQL is regional relational.
- **Cold classes are about price and minimum duration, not retrieval speed.** Rarely read, kept for years: Archive, plus a lifecycle rule to move data there.
- **Private Service Connect when ranges overlap or must not be coordinated;** VPC Peering needs non-overlapping, non-transitive connections.
- **Spot for fault-tolerant batch, CUDs for the steady baseline,** never CUDs for peak capacity and never Spot for work that cannot be interrupted.
- **Single anycast IP and nearest-healthy-region routing means a global external Application Load Balancer** (add Cloud CDN for cacheable content).
